athletic meet.meaning: A school sports day; students run and play games against each other.

fresh eyes.example: The house and the meadows that surrounded it were so much a part of her childhood, a part of her life, that she didn't often look at them with fresh eyes.

back and forth.example: She rocked gently back and forth in the old chair.

high holidays.meaning: the most holy days of the Jewish year
high holidays.example: On the New Year of the Jewish High Holidays in 1943, those who gathered to worship at the synagogue in Copenhagen, as the fictional Rosens did, were warned by the rabbi that they were to be taken and "relocated" by the Germans.

hand hemmed.meaning: sewn by hand along the edge of cloth
hand hemmed.example: The little hand-hemmed linen handkerchief that Annemarie carried to her uncle?

grow up.example: You should be an actress when you grow up.

paragraphs.context: have faded into a pleasant, undisturbed retirement on dusty library shelves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Most old books are forgotten, but this book is still loved.
paragraphs.simple: Most books written long ago are no longer read. They sit on library shelves and people forget them. It is as if they have stopped working, the way old people retire from their jobs. But Number the Stars is different. It is still full of life. Every single day, readers write to the author about it.

paragraphs.context: the right thing is often hard, sometimes dangerous, and frequently unpopular
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ten-year-olds want to do the right thing, but learn it can be hard and dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie is ten, and most readers of this book are about ten, too. At ten, young people start to think hard about right and wrong. They want to grow into honorable adults. They long to choose what is right. But they are beginning to learn a hard truth: choosing rightly is often difficult, sometimes perilous, and frequently unpopular — others may dislike you for it.

paragraphs.context: the soldiers were simply part of the landscape
paragraphs.mainIdea: Little Kirsti has always seen soldiers, so she does not fear them.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie and Ellen look straight ahead so the soldiers will not notice them. But little Kirsti runs ahead through the door, chattering happily. For Kirsti, soldiers on every corner are simply part of the street. She has seen them all her remembered life. To her they are as ordinary and unimportant as lampposts. This shows how long the occupation has lasted: Kirsti cannot remember a world without soldiers.

paragraphs.context: De Frie Danske—The Free Danes—was an illegal newspaper
paragraphs.mainIdea: The family secretly reads an illegal Resistance newspaper about attacks on the Nazis.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie listens while the mothers talk. She knows they mean De Frie Danske, which means The Free Danes. It is a newspaper the Germans have forbidden. Peter brings it to the family, folded and hidden inside ordinary books and papers. After Mama and Papa read it, Mama burns it so the Germans will never find it. The paper carries secret news of sabotage: explosives planted in German factories, and trains carrying war goods that were wrecked so the goods could not move.

paragraphs.context: The Resistance fighters were Danish people—no one knew who
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Resistance are secret brave Danes who damage the Nazis' war work.
paragraphs.simple: Papa has explained to Annemarie what the Resistance is. The Resistance fighters are Danish people. No one knows who they are, because they must stay very secret. They are determined to hurt the Nazis however they can. They damage German trucks and cars. They bomb German factories. They are very brave. Sometimes they are caught and killed.

paragraphs.context: He was not like fairy tale kings, who seemed to stand on balconies
paragraphs.mainIdea: The real King Christian is a kind, ordinary man, not like kings in stories.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie thinks about King Christian X, the real king of Denmark. He is not like the kings in fairy tales. In stories, kings stand up high and shout orders at their servants. They sit on gold chairs and hunt for husbands for their daughters. King Christian is a real man whose face looks serious and kind. Every morning he rides his horse alone through Copenhagen and greets his people. When Annemarie was little, Lise took her to wave at him, and sometimes he waved back and smiled.

paragraphs.context: Mama had been crocheting that evening three years ago
paragraphs.mainIdea: Three years ago Mama was making wedding things for Lise, who died before marrying Peter.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie remembers an evening three years ago. Mama sat across the room, using a needle to make a lacy edge for a pillowcase out of thin white thread. The pillowcase was part of Lise's trousseau — the clothes and linens a bride brings to her marriage. Lise was eighteen then and about to marry Peter Neilsen. Mama said that when they married, Annemarie and Kirsti would have a brother for the first time. But Lise died, and the wedding never happened.
paragraphs.grammar: Past perfect ('had been crocheting') puts Mama's action before the story's present — a memory inside a memory.

paragraphs.context: She imagined the pink strip of Norway crushed by a fist
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie pictures Norway, pink on her school map, crushed like paper by Germany.
paragraphs.simple: At school Annemarie saw a map on which Norway, above Denmark, was colored pink. Papa says Norway fought Germany fiercely but was crushed — beaten completely. In her mind, Annemarie sees the pink shape of Norway. She imagines a giant fist closing on it and squeezing it flat, the way a hand crushes paper. The fist is Germany: huge and strong. Small Norway could not win.

paragraphs.context: Once he had been like a fun-loving older brother
paragraphs.mainIdea: Since Lise's death, Peter has changed from playful to hurried and serious.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie thinks about how Peter has changed. Before Lise died, Peter was like a fun big brother to the girls. He teased them and tickled them. He was always joking and playing tricks. He sang silly songs that made Annemarie and Kirsti shriek with laughter. Now he still stops by and greets them warmly, but he is always in a hurry. He talks quickly to Mama and Papa about things Annemarie does not understand. He never sings the silly songs now, and he never stays long.

paragraphs.context: Our king was wise. He knew how few soldiers Denmark had.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Denmark surrendered because it was too small to fight Germany.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie asks why the king did not fight the Nazis. Papa sighs and explains. Denmark is such a tiny country, and Germany is such an enormous enemy. Their king was wise. He knew how few soldiers Denmark had. He knew that many, many Danish people would die if they fought. So the king chose surrender, to save people's lives.
paragraphs.grammar: 'Such a tiny country / such an enormous enemy': 'such a + adjective + noun' means 'so very' (strong emphasis).

paragraphs.context: it was a treat to see Peter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter's secret nighttime visit is frightening but joyful; he is like a son to the family.
paragraphs.simple: Late at night there is a light knock. It is Peter! He has come in the dark, which is dangerous, because no citizen may go out after eight o'clock — Copenhagen has a curfew. His visits are always hurried and seem secret in a way Annemarie cannot quite explain. Still, seeing Peter is a special joy. It reminds her of happier days. Mama and Papa love Peter like a son: he was going to marry their daughter Lise.

paragraphs.context: they want to torment Jewish people. It has happened in the other countries.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter explains the Nazis are starting to torment Jews in Denmark, as in other countries.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie asks why the button shop was closed. Peter leans forward and explains. Tormenting Jewish people — hurting them in small, cruel ways for no reason — is the Nazis' way. It has already happened in the other countries they occupy. In Denmark they took their time and let people relax a little. But now it seems to be starting here, too.

paragraphs.context: that people were called upon to be so brave
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie comforts herself that ordinary people are never asked to be heroes.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie asks herself, in the dark, whether she would truly die to protect the Jews. She is honest enough to admit she is not sure. For a moment she feels frightened. Then she pulls the blanket higher and relaxes. She tells herself it is all imaginary, not real. Such courage — giving your life for another person — happens only in made-up stories, she thinks. Not in real Denmark, and not to ordinary people like the Rosens and the Johansens. She is glad to be ordinary.

paragraphs.context: Mama had comforted her by calling it a birthday celebration
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama lied that the explosions were birthday fireworks to comfort frightened Kirsti.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie suddenly remembers a night a month ago. Kirsti's birthday is in late August. That night, Annemarie, too, woke up in fear at the noise of explosions. The sky in the southeast was ablaze with light. Mama sat on their bed, held the dark curtain aside, and comforted Kirsti by calling the lights a birthday celebration. Mama said, 'Just think — fireworks for a five-year-old's birthday!' It was not true — but the kind lie made Kirsti feel safe.

paragraphs.context: The Danes had destroyed their own naval fleet
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Danes sank their own warships so the Germans could not use them.
paragraphs.simple: The next evening's newspaper told the sad truth behind the 'fireworks.' The Danes had destroyed their own navy. As the Germans approached to take over the ships for their own use, the Danes blew up the vessels one by one. They chose to sink their own fleet rather than let the enemy sail it in the war.

paragraphs.context: to watch Mrs. Rosen light the Sabbath candles on Friday evenings
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girls respectfully watch the Rosens' Friday candle-lighting prayer, a Jewish custom.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie and Kirsti are often invited to watch Mrs. Rosen light the Sabbath candles on Friday evenings. Mrs. Rosen covers her head with a cloth. She says a special prayer in Hebrew, the old language of the Jewish people. Annemarie always stands very quietly, full of wonder. Even chatterbox little Kirsti stays completely quiet then. They do not understand the words, but they can feel what a special, holy time it is for the Rosen family.

paragraphs.context: We don't know where, and we don't really know why. They call it 'relocation.'
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Nazis use the mild word 'relocation' for arresting Jews; Papa says it is wrong and dangerous.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie asks where the Nazis will take the Jews. Papa shakes his head. No one can say where they will go, and no one truly knows the reason. The Nazis use a mild, harmless-sounding word for it: 'relocation,' as if families were simply moving to a new home. But no one knows what the word really hides. All they know is this: it is wrong, it is dangerous, and they must help.
paragraphs.grammar: The quotation marks around 'relocation' mark it as the Nazis' word, not Papa's — a euphemism he rejects.

paragraphs.context: The German occupation forces had burned part of it
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Germans burned part of Tivoli Gardens to punish the fun-loving Danes.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie tells Kirsti she never saw the Tivoli fireworks, because Tivoli Gardens is closed now. The German occupation forces burned part of it. Perhaps they did it to punish the Danes for loving fun and lighthearted pleasure. So the 'fireworks' Kirsti heard on her birthday were not fireworks at all — they were the explosions of the sinking Danish navy.

paragraphs.context: there had been an accident. Mama and Papa rushed to the hospital
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lise died after a nighttime accident; Mama and Papa rushed to the hospital.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie tells Ellen what little she knows about Lise's death. Lise and Peter were out together one evening. Then the telephone rang with news of an accident. Mama and Papa hurried to the hospital. Ellen's mother came to stay with Annemarie and little Kirsti. Kirsti was already asleep and slept right through everything. But Annemarie stayed up, and late that night her parents returned home and told her Lise had died.

paragraphs.context: Dangers were no more than odd imaginings, like ghost stories
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie feels completely safe, believing danger is only imaginary like ghost stories.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie lies in bed feeling safe and comfortable. Her parents are in the next room. Her best friend sleeps beside her. She thinks dangers are no more than strange imaginings — like the ghost stories children make up to frighten one another. Things that could not possibly happen. She yawns contentedly and closes her eyes, feeling completely safe in her own home.

paragraphs.context: why Papa had torn them from the book
paragraphs.mainIdea: Papa tore out the photos to hide the dates that would show Lise's real age.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie suddenly understands, with cold fear, why Papa tore the three photographs out of the album. Under each baby photograph, Mama had written the child's name in her delicate handwriting. But each page also carried a written date beneath the photograph. And the real Lise Johansen was born twenty-one years earlier. If the officer read the date, he would know the ten-year-old 'Lise' is a lie. Papa tore out the pictures to hide the dates.

paragraphs.context: she will be bringing you a carton of cigarettes
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the phone Papa uses code: 'a carton of cigarettes' means Ellen, a Jewish child.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie listens, puzzled, while Papa talks cheerfully to Uncle Henrik on the telephone. Papa says Mama is bringing 'a carton of cigarettes.' This cannot be true: there are no cigarettes in the stores, and Papa complains constantly about missing them. He is speaking in code. The 'carton of cigarettes' is Ellen — one Jewish child Mama is bringing to Henrik tonight. 'A lot of cigarettes in Copenhagen' means many more Jewish people will follow.

paragraphs.context: as if I might come upon Trofast, waiting still, with his tail wagging
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama still half-expects her long-dead childhood dog Trofast to be waiting on the path.
paragraphs.simple: Mama tells the girls about her childhood dog. She named him Trofast, which means Faithful, and it was the right name: every afternoon he waited on this path for her to come home from school. Even today, Mama says, when she comes around the bend, she feels as if she might find Trofast still waiting there, his tail wagging. The path is empty today — no people, no faithful dog — but the memory is so strong that Mama can almost see him.

paragraphs.context: They relocate all the farmers' butter, right into the stomach of their army!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama jokes that the Germans 'relocate' butter into their army's stomachs.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie makes a joke: do the soldiers 'relocate' butter, too? Mama laughs ruefully and says yes. The Germans take all the farmers' butter to feed their army. Her bitter joke turns the Nazis' own mild word against them: the butter is 'relocated' straight into German soldiers' bellies! She adds that if the Germans knew Henrik had saved a little butter, armed soldiers would march down the path and seize it.

paragraphs.context: the specter of guns and grim-faced soldiers seemed nothing more than a ghost story
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the sunny kitchen, the war feels unreal, like a ghost story for children.
paragraphs.simple: It is a bright, happy morning in the farmhouse kitchen. Cream stands in a pitcher. A bird sings in the apple tree by the door. Out on the water, Uncle Henrik pulls in nets of shining fish under a blue sky. In this warm, safe moment, guns and stern-faced soldiers feel unreal — like a made-up scary tale told to frighten children at bedtime. But the feeling is false: the danger is real, and it will come tonight.

paragraphs.context: Papa had said something like it on the telephone
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie realizes 'a day for fishing' is the same secret code Papa used.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Henrik says, 'Tomorrow will be a day for fishing,' and his smile disappears. Annemarie recognizes the strange phrase. On the telephone, Papa asked Henrik, 'Is the weather good for fishing?' But what can it mean? Henrik goes fishing every day, rain or shine; Danish fishermen do not wait for sunny days. So 'a day for fishing' cannot really be about fishing — it must be another secret code, like Papa's.

paragraphs.context: It is the old custom, you know, for the dead to rest at home
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik says the family will hold a traditional wake for the invented Great-aunt Birte.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Henrik tells the girls there has been a death. Tonight their Great-aunt Birte — a very, very old woman — will lie in her casket in the living room through the night, ahead of the next day’s burial. He explains the old custom: the dead person lies at home, and family and friends keep the body company until the funeral. Annemarie is confused: she has never heard of any Great-aunt Birte, and strangely, no one seems sad.

paragraphs.context: it is much easier to be brave if you do not know everything
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik teaches Annemarie the book's key lesson: it is easier to be brave without full knowledge.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Henrik tells Annemarie something she must understand. Courage comes more easily when you do not know the whole terrible truth. That is why Mama does not know everything, and neither does he. They know only what they need to know. If you knew how great the danger was, fear might stop you. Knowing less lets you simply do what must be done. This is why the grown-ups keep secrets from Annemarie: to protect her, and to help her be brave.

paragraphs.context: she was protecting Ellen the way her mother had protected her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie chooses to lie to Ellen, protecting her friend as Mama protected her.
paragraphs.simple: Ellen says she is sorry about 'Aunt Birte,' and Mama thanks her sadly. Annemarie says nothing. She thinks: now I, too, am lying — and to my very best friend. She could whisper the secret so Ellen would not feel sad. But she does not. She understands at last: she is shielding her friend just as Mama shielded her. It is better and safer for Ellen to believe in Great-aunt Birte. So Annemarie stays silent — she has become a protector, like the grown-ups.

paragraphs.context: these people had nothing to talk about
paragraphs.mainIdea: The 'mourners' cannot talk because there are no real memories of the invented aunt.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie remembers Lise's funeral in Copenhagen: friends came every evening, brought food so Mama would not need to cook, and talked softly about Lise, remembering happier times. But tonight's visitors brought no food and do not talk. Slicing cheese in the kitchen, Annemarie works it out: these people have nothing to talk about. They cannot remember happy times with Great-aunt Birte — because there never was a Great-aunt Birte at all.

paragraphs.context: it was as if Ellen had moved now into a different world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie feels Ellen slipping into a different world — her family's world of danger.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie looks at Ellen sitting between her parents, one hand held tight in her mother's. She feels a wave of sadness. The bond of their friendship is not broken. But it is as if Ellen has moved into a different world now — her family’s world, and whatever frightening things await them. Annemarie is still in the safe world of childhood; Ellen has been pulled into the dangerous grown-up world.

paragraphs.context: there was a chance the germs would still be there, would still be dangerous
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama invents a clever lie about typhus germs to keep the casket closed.
paragraphs.simple: The officer demands that the casket be opened for a last look at Great-aunt Birte. Mama walks straight to the casket and agrees at once — too eagerly. She makes up a story on the spot: a doctor ordered the coffin shut because the old woman died of typhus, a spreading sickness, and the sickness might still live in the dead body and still be dangerous. But what does a foolish old country doctor know? Surely no germs can live in a dead person! Let us open it! Disgusted, the officer refuses — and Mama's trick works.

paragraphs.context: when they protected one another by not telling
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie learns the Resistance rule: people protect each other by not asking and not telling.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie watches Mr. Rosen slide the packet into his pocket without asking what is inside. She understands: this is how they guard each other — by keeping secrets. If Mr. Rosen knew the packet's secret, the knowledge could terrify him. And knowing could put him in worse danger. So he did not ask, and Peter did not explain. Not knowing keeps everyone safer.

paragraphs.context: he had moved beyond his own youth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter calling Mama 'Inge' shows he has become a grown man in a dangerous world.
paragraphs.simple: Saying goodbye, Peter calls Annemarie's mother 'Inge' — her first name. Annemarie realizes she has never heard him do that before. He always said 'Mrs. Johansen.' In the old happy days of his engagement to Lise, he sometimes called her 'Mama.' Now it is 'Inge.' It is as if Peter has stepped out of boyhood into the grown-up world. He is no longer the playful almost-brother; he is a serious Resistance man, perhaps saying a last goodbye.

paragraphs.context: their shoulders were as straight as they had been in the past
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Rosens keep their dignity: pride lives in them, not in the things they left behind.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie looks at the Rosens in shabby borrowed clothes, holding rough blankets, their faces drawn and tired. She remembers happier times: Mrs. Rosen lighting the Sabbath candles, Mr. Rosen reading his thick books, Ellen acting confidently on the school stage. All those proud things — the candlesticks, the books, the theater dreams — stayed behind in Copenhagen. But the Rosens sit with straight shoulders, as always. Dignity lives inside them: the most important things came with them.

paragraphs.context: Dawn would creep across the Swedish farmland and coast
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dawn is pictured as a living thing creeping across Sweden, Denmark, and Norway.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie wakes and sees the first pale light at the meadow's edge. The author pictures the dawn as if it were alive. Morning light crawls slowly over Sweden's fields and shores. Next it pours over tiny Denmark. Then it crosses the North Sea to rouse Norway. Three countries, one sunrise: even in wartime, the new day comes to everyone.

paragraphs.context: to the cabin that they were invisible in an instant
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama reports Henrik hid the Rosens below deck so fast they vanished instantly.
paragraphs.simple: Mama tells Annemarie what happened at the boat. Though it was still dark and the Rosens did not know the path, they reached the harbor quickly. Henrik was waiting on the boat. He took them aboard and down below into the cabin so fast that they vanished in an instant — no watcher could have seen them. Peter, she adds, had already brought the other group there safely, too.

paragraphs.context: you must pretend to be nothing more than a little girl
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mama gives Annemarie her cover story: a silly girl bringing lunch to her uncle.
paragraphs.simple: Mama warns Annemarie how dangerous the trip is. If soldiers stop her, she must play the part of a foolish child who knows nothing. Her cover story: she is carrying food to her forgetful fisherman uncle, who left his lunch at home. She must act empty-headed and silly. Being a harmless little girl is her only protection.

paragraphs.context: She heard bushes rustling ahead. She heard footsteps.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Like Red Riding Hood hearing the wolf, Annemarie hears real danger: the soldiers' dogs.
paragraphs.simple: On the dark path, Annemarie has been telling herself the story of Little Red Riding-Hood, who carried a basket of food through the woods. In the story, Red Riding-Hood hears a noise in the bushes — it is the wolf. Now Annemarie stops on the real path. New sounds reach her: leaves shaking ahead, steps, and — impossible to mistake — a low growl. The fairy-tale wolf has become real: around the turn wait four armed soldiers with two large dogs.

paragraphs.context: Annemarie tried to giggle, the way her sister might
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annemarie bravely acts like silly little Kirsti to fool the soldiers.
paragraphs.simple: The soldier demands why she came before daybreak just to bring a lunch. Annemarie thinks: what would Kirsti say? She forces out a giggle, copying her little sister. She chatters away: Uncle Henrik doesn't even like fish — he sees too much of it! She makes a face. Inside she is terrified, but she performs the silly-little-girl part perfectly, and the soldier starts to believe her.

paragraphs.context: That's all that brave means—not thinking about the dangers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Henrik defines bravery: not thinking of danger, only of what you must do.
paragraphs.simple: Annemarie insists she was not brave — she was frightened. Uncle Henrik smiles and stops her. Bravery, he says, is simply this: you don't dwell on the perils; you fix your mind on the job in front of you. Of course you were frightened — he was frightened today, too. But she kept her mind on what she had to do. Being brave does not mean feeling no fear. It means doing what must be done although you are afraid.

paragraphs.context: Many of the fishermen have built hidden places in their boats
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fishermen built hidden compartments under deck boards to smuggle Jews to Sweden.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Henrik tells Annemarie a little of the secret. Many fishermen — Henrik included — have made secret compartments under their boats' floors. Lift the right boards, and a few people can crouch unseen below deck. Peter and others in the Resistance bring the Jewish people to Henrik and the other fishermen. And all along the road to Gilleleje, helpers shelter them and guide them onward. It is a whole secret network.

paragraphs.context: when they sniff at it, it ruins their sense of smell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Scientists made a powder that attracts dogs but destroys their sense of smell.
paragraphs.simple: Uncle Henrik explains the handkerchief's secret. The soldiers have begun using trained dogs to sniff out hidden people on the boats. Peter took the problem to scientists and doctors, who worked night and day. They made a special drug — a powder hidden in the handkerchief. The powder draws the dogs in, then wrecks their noses, so they cannot smell anything else — not the hidden people.

paragraphs.context: Peter Neilsen was dead. It was a painful fact to recall
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the joyful day of liberation, Annemarie mourns Peter, executed by the Germans.
paragraphs.simple: The war is over and all Denmark is celebrating. But amid the joy, Annemarie makes herself face a heartbreaking truth: Peter Neilsen is dead. The Germans captured him and executed him — killed him as punishment — at Ryvangen in Copenhagen, before a crowd. On this day of happiness, she remembers her redheaded almost-brother and how terrible the news was.

paragraphs.context: they had laid flowers there, on the bleak, numbered ground
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Nazis buried executed men in numbered graves; Annemarie learns the truth about Lise.
paragraphs.simple: The Nazis would not give back the bodies of the young men they shot at Ryvangen. They buried them where they fell and marked each grave with only a number — no name. Later, Annemarie went there with Mama and Papa and left flowers on the bare earth where each grave bore only a number. That night, her parents finally revealed what really happened to Lise when the war began.

paragraphs.context: The people would have been destroyed had they tried to defend themselves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Denmark surrendered in 1940 because fighting Germany would have destroyed the small country.
paragraphs.simple: In the Afterword the author gives the real history. Denmark surrendered to Germany in 1940, for the reasons Papa gave Annemarie: the country was tiny and defenseless, with hardly any army at all. If tiny Denmark had fought the mighty German forces, its people would have been wiped out. So King Christian surrendered, with great sorrow, and overnight the soldiers moved in. For five years they occupied Denmark and controlled almost everything — but they never controlled the king.
paragraphs.grammar: 'Had they tried' = 'if they had tried': dropping 'if' and moving the verb first makes a formal conditional (inversion).

paragraphs.context: was smuggled across the sea to Sweden
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nearly 7,000 Danish Jews were smuggled across the sea to safety in Sweden.
paragraphs.simple: In the weeks after the Jewish New Year, close to seven thousand Jews — nearly every Jewish person in Denmark — were secretly carried by boat to Sweden. The Danes took the Jews in, fed them, clothed them, hid them, and helped them along to safety. It was one of the great rescues of the war: an entire country's Jewish people saved by their neighbors.

paragraphs.context: Swedish scientists worked swiftly to prevent such detection
paragraphs.mainIdea: The handkerchief drug is real history: Swedish scientists made a smell-destroying powder.
paragraphs.simple: Was the handkerchief just the author's invention, to make a heroine of a little girl? No — it is part of real history. After the Nazis began using police dogs to find hidden people on the fishing boats, Swedish scientists worked swiftly. They mixed a strong powder from dried rabbit's blood and cocaine. The blood lured the dogs close; the cocaine deadened their noses, killing their ability to smell for a time. Almost every boat captain carried such a handkerchief. The trick saved many lives.

paragraphs.context: must be to create an ideal of human decency
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kim's last letter asks people to dream of a world of human decency, not prejudice.
paragraphs.simple: The author closes with words written by Kim Malthe-Bruun, a real twenty-one-year-old Resistance fighter, in a letter to his mother the night before the Nazis killed him. He begs everyone to remember: do not wish to go back to the days before the war. Instead, young and old alike should dream of building a world where people act with true kindness and fairness — free of small-minded hate. That dream of a decent world, he says, is the great gift every country hungers for.

sentences.context: Her voice trailed away, the sentence unfinished.
sentences.simple: She stopped talking in the middle of her sentence; she did not finish it.
sentences.grammar: 'The sentence unfinished' has no verb — it is an absolute phrase describing the situation (the sentence = left unfinished).

sentences.context: All of Denmark is his bodyguard.
sentences.simple: All the Danish people together protect the king, as one bodyguard would.
sentences.grammar: 'Bodyguard' is singular but means all the people acting as one protector — a metaphor, not a real bodyguard.

sentences.context: It was so like Peter, to bring just the right gift.
sentences.simple: Bringing exactly the right gift is just what Peter would do; it is typical of him.
sentences.grammar: 'So like someone, to do something' = that behavior is typical of that person.

sentences.context: all of Denmark must be bodyguard for the Jews, as well
sentences.simple: All Danish people together must protect the Jews, the way one bodyguard protects a person.
sentences.grammar: 'Be bodyguard' (no 'a') treats all of Denmark as one single protector.

sentences.context: people were called upon to be so brave
sentences.simple: People were asked to be that brave only in fairy tales — never in real life.
sentences.grammar: Cleft sentence 'It was only in X that...' puts strong emphasis on 'only in fairy tales.'

sentences.context: to picture the tall, aging king
sentences.simple: Imagining the old king, perhaps with tears in his eyes, looking at his sunken, broken navy, made Annemarie feel both sad and proud.
sentences.grammar: 'Which now lay submerged and broken' is a relative clause describing the navy ('lay' = was lying, sunk under water).

sentences.context: Once I had three daughters. Tonight I am proud to have three daughters again.
sentences.simple: Papa once had three daughters, but Lise died. Tonight Ellen becomes his third daughter again.
sentences.grammar: 'Again' points back to Lise — the family is whole once more, with Ellen in Lise's place.

sentences.context: the rain made it seem as if the whole world was crying
sentences.simple: The rain looked as if the whole world were crying with sadness, like Mama.
sentences.grammar: 'As if' + past tense ('was crying') describes something imagined, not real.

sentences.context: From a different father? From the milkman?
sentences.simple: The officer cruelly suggests Ellen is not Papa's child but the milkman's — an insult hinting Mama was unfaithful.
sentences.grammar: The old 'milkman joke': claiming a child resembles the milkman hints the mother had an affair.

sentences.context: seagulls soared and cried out as if they were mourning
sentences.simple: The crying seagulls sounded like people mourning — weeping sadly at a funeral.
sentences.grammar: 'As if they were mourning' paints the birds' cries as human grief (past 'were' marks it imagined).

sentences.context: it would not have been so easy to be brave.
sentences.simple: If Annemarie had known the full danger that day, being brave would have been much harder.
sentences.grammar: 'If she had known' (past perfect) imagines a past that did not happen — a counterfactual condition.

sentences.context: It is Great-aunt Birte, who never was.
sentences.simple: The 'dead aunt' never existed; Henrik invented her as a cover story.
sentences.grammar: 'Who never was' = who never existed — a short, wry way to say she is fictional.

sentences.context: In that moment, with that look, they became equals.
sentences.simple: In that silent look, mother and daughter became equals — Annemarie is now treated as a grown-up who shares the secret.
sentences.grammar: 'Equals' = two people on the same level: no longer just parent and child, but partners.

sentences.context: To be brave came more easily if you knew nothing.
sentences.simple: It is easier to be brave when you do not know how great the danger is.
sentences.grammar: The infinitive 'To be brave' works as the sentence's subject (= 'Being brave came...').

sentences.context: he who numbers the stars one by one
sentences.simple: God counts every star in the sky, one after another. (This line gives the book its title.)
sentences.grammar: 'He who' = 'the one who' — an old, formal way to say 'the person who.'

sentences.context: The sky was, too, thought Annemarie.
sentences.simple: The sky was too cold and too big, too, Annemarie thought — and the whole world was too cruel.
sentences.grammar: Inverted reporting clause ('thought Annemarie' after the words); 'was, too' borrows 'too cold and too big' from the sentence before.

sentences.context: It was only a brief grasp at something that had gone.
sentences.simple: Peter's joke was a small, sad attempt to hold onto the happy old days, which are gone forever.
sentences.grammar: No special grammar — 'grasp at' (trying to hold) is used figuratively, for trying to keep the past.

sentences.context: It was harder for the ones who were waiting
sentences.simple: Waiting was harder than acting: those who wait face less danger but feel more fear.
sentences.grammar: 'Less danger, perhaps, but more fear' leaves out 'there was' — a compact contrast of two short phrases.

sentences.context: it was a sleep as thin as the night clouds
sentences.simple: She fell into a very light sleep, easily broken — as thin and fragile as the clouds.
sentences.grammar: 'As thin as the night clouds' is a simile comparing her light sleep to thin clouds.

sentences.context: forcing her eyes to understand, needing to understand, not wanting to understand
sentences.simple: She forced herself to look and needed to know, but she was afraid of what she would see.
sentences.grammar: Three parallel -ing phrases build her fear step by step: forcing, needing, not wanting.

sentences.context: did Annemarie realize how cold the dawn was
sentences.simple: Only when she entered the woods did Annemarie realize how cold the dawn was.
sentences.grammar: After a limiting opener like 'Only now,' subject and verb swap places ('did Annemarie realize' = 'Annemarie realized') — inversion for emphasis.

sentences.context: Annemarie willed herself, with all her being, to behave as Kirsti would.
sentences.simple: With all her strength of will, Annemarie forced herself to act the way Kirsti would act.
sentences.grammar: 'Willed herself to behave' = forced herself by strong will; 'with all her being' = with everything in her.

sentences.context: Your army eats all of Denmark's meat.
sentences.simple: She boldly tells the soldier the rude truth: the German army takes all of Denmark's meat.
sentences.grammar: Simple present ('eats') for a repeated, habitual truth — said straight to the soldier's face (brave rudeness).

sentences.context: Suddenly, to her own surprise, she begin to cry.
sentences.simple: To her own surprise, real tears came — she was not acting; the tears were real, and they saved her.
sentences.grammar: Note: the book prints 'begin' where the past tense 'began' would be expected.

sentences.context: His voice trailed off, and he didn't finish the sentence.
sentences.simple: He stopped talking without saying the terrible ending: without the handkerchief, they would all have been caught. He didn't need to say it.
sentences.grammar: The unfinished sentence leaves the frightening result unsaid — everyone understands it anyway.

sentences.context: If she had not found the packet where Mr. Rosen had dropped it.
sentences.simple: She pictures what almost happened: if she had not found the packet, not run through the woods, not reached the boat in time — all would have been lost.
sentences.grammar: 'If she had not found' (past perfect) imagines a past that almost happened; 'all of the ifs' = all the things that could have gone wrong.

sentences.context: From the military car, they saw her running, and simply ran her down.
sentences.simple: The Nazis in the military car saw Lise running and deliberately drove into her and killed her. It was murder, not an accident.
sentences.grammar: 'Run down' = hit with a vehicle; 'simply' shows cold, casual cruelty.

sentences.context: The people would have been destroyed had they tried to defend themselves
sentences.simple: If the Danish people had tried to fight, they would have been destroyed by the huge German forces.
sentences.grammar: 'Had they tried' = 'if they had tried': in formal conditionals 'if' can drop and the verb moves first (inversion).

sentences.context: After a while even courage becomes routine to the reader.
sentences.simple: When you read many brave stories one after another, bravery starts to feel ordinary — which is why the photograph shocked her so deeply.
sentences.grammar: No special grammar — the power is in the idea: 'routine' (ordinary, everyday) is a shocking word for 'courage.'
